text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
notes: The Hebrew word "אֱלֹהִים" (Elohim) is rendered as "God" to reflect the singular theological sense, despite its plural form.
The term "הַשָּׁמַיִם" is translated as "the heavens" to preserve the plural sense of the Hebrew, which can encompass the sky, the cosmos, or the divine realm.
The particle "אֵת" is a direct‑object marker and is omitted in the English rendering.

text: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
notes: "רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים" is rendered as "the spirit of God" per the terminology policy. The Hebrew verb "מְרַחֶפֶת" is translated as "moved" to preserve the sense of motion without adding interpretive nuance. The phrase "תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ" is rendered literally as "without form and void" rather than the more interpretive "formless and empty" to remain conservative.

text: And God said, let there be light; and there was light.
notes: The Hebrew phrase "וְהִי אֱלֹהִים" is rendered as "God" per the terminology policy.
The clause "let there be light" is an imperative, indicating a divine command.
The subsequent clause "and there was light" records the immediate result of that command.

text: God saw the light, because it was good, and God separated the light from the darkness.
God called the light Day. He called the darkness Night. Evening and morning marked the first day.
notes: Day and Night are treated as proper nouns.

text: God said, let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.
God made the firmament. He separated the waters below the firmament from the waters above it. It was so.
notes: ‘firmament’ is the chosen rendering for רָקִיעַ.

text: God called the firmament Heaven. And evening and morning were the second day.
God said: gather the waters beneath the heavens into one place, and let dry land appear. It happened.
notes: The Hebrew phrase "תחת השמים" literally means "under the heavens".

text: And God called the dry land Earth; and the gathering of the waters he called Seas; and God saw that it was good.
notes: The Hebrew phrase 'מִקְוֵה הַמַּיִם' is rendered as 'the gathering of the waters'.

text: God said, let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree bearing fruit after its kind, whose seed is within itself, on the earth. And it was so.
The earth produced grass, herb that yields seed of its kind, and trees that bear fruit with seed in them, of their kind. God saw that it was good.
Evening and morning were the third day.
And God said, let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate day from night; let them be for signs, for seasons, for days, and for years.
Let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to illuminate the earth. It was so.
notes: expanse chosen for clarity over the archaic term 'firmament'.

text: God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.
And God placed them in the expanse of the heavens to give light to the earth.
notes: ‘expanse’ is a modern rendering of the Hebrew ‘רְקִיעַ’, traditionally translated as ‘firmament’.

text: And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide between the light and the darkness, and God saw that it was good.
notes: The Hebrew phrase 'וְלִמְשֹׁל' is rendered as 'to rule' rather than 'to reign'.

text: Evening came, and morning came, the fourth day.
And God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth upon the expanse of heaven.
notes: שֶׁרֶץ rendered as "living creature" to convey the Hebrew sense of a creature with life.
רְקִיעַ rendered as "expanse" rather than "firmament" for a modern, precise description.

text: God created the great whales. He also created every living creature that moves, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after its kind. He created every winged fowl after its kind. God saw that it was good.
notes: The Hebrew term תַּנִּינִם is rendered as "whales"; the adjective גְּדֹלִים is translated as "great".
"After its kind" follows the Hebrew phrase לְמִינֵהוּ, indicating the classification of each group.

text: And God blessed them, saying, Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.
notes: The phrase "וְהָ/ע֖וֹף יִ֥רֶב" is rendered as "let birds multiply" to reflect the imperative sense of the Hebrew verb.

text: Evening and morning marked the fifth day.
And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures of its kind: cattle and creeping things, and beasts of the earth of its kind." And it was so.
God made the beasts of the earth according to their kind, the cattle according to their kind, and all the creeping things of the earth according to their kind. God saw that it was good.
notes: The Hebrew phrase "לְמִינָהּ" is rendered as "according to their kind" to convey the sense of classification.

text: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the fowl of the air, over the cattle, over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.
notes: The pronoun "them" refers to the plural "us" used in the verse.

text: God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him. He created male and female.
notes: The Hebrew phrase 'בְּצֶ֥לֶם אֱלֹהִ֖ים' is a double image clause; it is rendered as 'in the image of God'.

text: God blessed them. God said to them: Be fruitful and multiply. Fill the earth and subdue it. Reign over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all living creatures that move on the earth.
notes: The Hebrew verb 'וּרְד֞וּ' is rendered as 'reign over' to convey the sense of dominion.

text: God said, "Behold, I have given you every herb that bears seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree that bears fruit and seed; it will be for your food."
notes: The phrase "זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע" is rendered as "bears seed" to convey the idea of seed-bearing plants.
The Hebrew term "עֵץ זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע" is translated as "tree that bears fruit and seed" to reflect the dual nature of fruit and seed-bearing trees.

text: God gave every green herb to every beast of the earth, every fowl of the air, and every creature that creeps on the earth where there is life, for food. And it was so.
notes: The original Hebrew uses the archaic verb ‘creepeth’; it has been rendered as ‘creeps’ for modern clarity.
The first-person pronoun ‘I’ has been replaced with ‘God’ to avoid archaic language while preserving the divine speaker.

text: God saw everything he had made, and behold, it was very good. The evening and the morning marked the sixth day.
